questions.q: How is "out-of-order" arrival different from the lateness a watermark handles?
options: Out-of-order events arrive within the watermark's tolerance, just not in the sequence they actually happened in — a distinct problem from arriving too late entirely
They're exactly the same problem with two different names
Out-of-order events are always dropped, while late events are always kept
Watermarks handle out-of-order events, and lateness is a separate KQL-only concept
questions.explain: A network retry or two producers writing near-simultaneously can cause event #2 to arrive before event #1, even safely inside the watermark's grace period.

questions.q: What does ingestion_time() - EventTime reveal in KQL?
options: How stale each event was on arrival — the gap between when it happened and when the system received it
The total row count of a table
Whether a window has closed yet
The Fabric Capacity SKU currently in use
questions.explain: This makes the arrival gap visible, which is the first step before deciding whether it's a meaningful problem.

questions.q: Why isn't "just sort by EventTime" a real fix for out-of-order arrival in an open window?
options: A window's running aggregate already includes whatever events arrived so far, in whatever order — sorting only helps display a finished result, not how the computation happened
KQL doesn't support the order by operator
Sorting always changes the underlying data values
It is actually a complete fix and no other approach is needed
questions.explain: Sorting is a display-time fix; it doesn't retroactively change how an in-progress aggregation already processed events.

questions.q: For which kind of aggregation does out-of-order arrival genuinely not matter?
options: A count() or sum() — the aggregate comes out the same regardless of arrival order
A running balance that depends on sequence
A sequence-number validation check
None — order always matters for every aggregation
questions.explain: Most of this chapter's aggregations (count, sum, avg) don't depend on the order events arrived in.

questions.q: What's one practical option for genuinely problematic out-of-order events, like ones failing a sequence check?
options: Route them to a distinct destination for manual review, using Eventstream routing logic
Always drop them silently with no record
Ignore the problem entirely, since KQL has no way to detect it
Convert them to batch ingestion instead of streaming
questions.explain: This uses the same Eventstream routing-to-multiple-destinations pattern covered in Lesson 36.
